teaching.text: A **mass-spring system** combines a mass that can move with a spring that pulls or pushes it toward **equilibrium**, its resting position.
children: Stretching the spring creates a restoring pull toward equilibrium. Compressing it creates a push in the opposite direction. In both cases, the force acts toward the resting position.
The mass has **inertia**. Once it is moving, its motion continues, so reaching equilibrium does not mean it stops there.

teaching.text: Pull the mass away from equilibrium and release it. The spring pulls it back, but the moving mass passes the resting position and compresses the spring on the other side.
children: The compressed spring pushes it back again. Continued motion and the restoring force produce the repeating back-and-forth movement called **vibration**.
This idealized model leaves friction out. It isolates what the mass and spring contribute to the motion.

teaching.text: In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves **along the spring line**, left and right. In **transverse motion**, it moves **across the spring line**, up and down between two supports.
children: Pulling the transverse mass upward extends the supporting springs. Their restoring pull brings it toward the middle, and its continued motion carries it through the middle to the other side.
The **m** on the moving object names its mass. The guide through the center marks its equilibrium position.

teaching.text: The two systems have the same mass and total restoring stiffness, so they repeat at the **same frequency**. Their directions differ, while the explanation of the cycle is the same.
children: The mass continues moving, and the springs act to restore equilibrium. Both properties are needed to explain why the system keeps passing through its resting position.

coverage.idea: Restoring force from stretching/compressing and equilibrium
Inertia and passage through equilibrium produce vibration
Longitudinal and transverse movement directions
Transverse restoring action and matching frequency
Mass identifier and equilibrium guide

teaching.text: **Frequency** is the number of complete back-and-forth cycles in a second. The two properties compared are **mass**, written **m**, and **total restoring stiffness**, written **K**. Stiffness describes how strongly the spring pushes or pulls back for a given displacement.
The **Reference** row supplies the starting condition, with mass m and stiffness K. Each of the other rows changes one property and leaves the other unchanged, making its effect on the rate clear.
The **Bigger mass** row uses **4m**, four times the reference mass, while stiffness remains K. A heavier mass is harder to turn around, so a complete cycle takes longer.
children: The result is **half the reference frequency**. Half the rate means half as many complete cycles in the same time, rather than half as much distance traveled.

teaching.text: The **Stiffer spring** row keeps mass m and uses **4K**, four times the reference stiffness. The stronger restoring pull turns the mass around sooner.
children: The result is **twice the reference frequency**, or twice as many cycles in the same time. Raising mass and raising stiffness therefore affect frequency in opposite directions.

teaching.text: The longitudinal and transverse versions match within every row. **More mass lowers frequency, and more stiffness raises frequency**, whichever direction the mass moves.

coverage.idea: Frequency means cycles per second
Reference mass/stiffness and controlled comparisons
4m at unchanged K produces half frequency and why
4K at unchanged m produces twice frequency and why
Mass and stiffness effects apply in both movement directions

teaching.text: Two equal masses are connected by a middle spring, with an outer spring connecting each mass to a fixed wall. The **1 and 2 on the objects identify the masses**. A **mode** is a pattern of vibration of the whole connected system.
In **mode 1**, both masses move **together**. They rise and fall together during transverse motion, or move left and right together during longitudinal motion.
children: Their separation stays the same, so the **middle spring does not stretch or compress**. The two outer springs do change length and supply the restoring pull.
The middle spring remains physically present, but its stiffness does not contribute through stretching or compression in this pattern.

teaching.text: In **mode 2**, the masses move **against each other**. One rises while the other falls, or they move toward and away from one another along the spring line.
children: Their changing separation stretches and compresses the middle spring. **All three springs now contribute to the restoring action.**
**Mode 2 has the higher frequency** because it uses more stiffness. The individual masses and springs have not changed; the two patterns use those parts differently.

teaching.text: Both modes can occur **at the same time**. Starting both masses on the same side of equilibrium, but at different displacements, gives movement that is partly together and partly against each other.
children: Adding the motion from both modes at every instant produces the **Both modes** row. Some moments have the masses moving in the same direction, while other moments have them moving against each other.
The combined movement contains two frequencies. It is a combination of the two modes, rather than a third independent mode.

coverage.idea: Two-mass three-spring setup and whole-system mode meaning
Mode 1 movement and inactive middle-spring stretching
Mode 2 opposing movement and middle-spring restoring action
Greater use of stiffness causes mode 2 higher frequency
Simultaneous modes and combined motion

teaching.text: A system with **three masses has three modes**. Each mode describes how all three masses move relative to one another, rather than assigning a separate mode to each mass.

In **mode 1**, all three masses move in the same direction. This is the lowest-frequency pattern because neighboring masses move mostly together and the connecting springs undergo relatively little stretching.

In **mode 2**, the middle mass stays still while the two outer masses move against each other. One outer mass moves up while the other moves down, or they move in opposite directions along the spring line.
children: This pattern can be started by leaving the middle mass undisturbed and moving the two outer masses in opposite directions. The stationary middle mass remains part of the three-mass system.

teaching.text: In **mode 3**, the middle mass moves against the two outer masses. The outer masses move together in one direction while the middle mass moves in the other.
children: This creates the strongest opposing movement between neighbors and the most stretching and compression. The restoring action is strongest, so mode 3 has the highest frequency.

teaching.text: The frequency comparison depends on **how the springs are used**, not on replacing them with different springs.
children: With two masses, moving together leaves the middle spring unchanged in length, while opposing movement stretches and compresses it. That extra restoring action explains why the opposing two-mass mode is faster.
With three masses, the same reasoning distinguishes the relatively gentle movement of mode 1 from the stronger relative movement of the higher modes.

coverage.idea: Actual spoken three-mass quiz has three modes
Three-mass mode 1 together and low frequency
Three-mass mode 2 still center and opposed outer masses
Three-mass mode 3 center opposes outer masses and high frequency
Spring participation explains frequency without altered parts

teaching.text: A **three-mass system has three modes**, each with a different movement pattern and frequency. The numbers **1, 2 and 3 on the objects** identify the masses; the row numbers identify whole-system modes.

In **mode 1**, all three masses move together. Neighboring masses have relatively little movement against one another, so there is less stretching of the connecting springs and the frequency is lowest.
children: Moving together describes their direction through the cycle. It does not require every mass to move exactly the same distance.

teaching.text: In **mode 2**, the middle mass stays still and the outer masses move against each other. The two sides can keep moving while the forces on the center balance.
children: The still center does not remove the middle mass or turn the system into a two-mass system. It describes how that mass participates in this particular mode.

teaching.text: In **mode 3**, the center moves against both outer masses. The outer masses rise as the center falls, and reverse together on the return movement.
children: This produces more stretching and compression than the lower modes, so **mode 3 has the highest frequency**. The parts have the same masses and stiffnesses across all three modes.

teaching.text: Several modes can occur together. The **All three** row adds the motion of the three pure modes at every point, producing a more complicated movement with three frequencies.
children: A pure mode is one of the system’s individual vibration patterns. A combination contains those existing patterns rather than creating an extra mode.

teaching.text: **Exciting a mode** means starting motion in that pattern. How a string is plucked or a violin is bowed changes which modes receive stronger motion.
children: Instrument control therefore includes favoring some vibration patterns over others. A trained singer also controls the vibrating vocal folds through their mass and stiffness.

coverage.idea: Three masses and three independent whole-system patterns
First mode together with relatively little internal stretching
Second mode still middle and opposed outer masses
Third mode center opposes both outer masses
Frequency order follows relative stretching and restoring action
All-three superposition is not another independent mode
Exciting modes in music and vocal-fold control

teaching.text: For these chains, **N masses give N independent modes**. N counts the masses. A one-mass system has one mode, a two-mass system has two, and a six-mass system has six.
children: Each row shows one chain with a particular number of masses. Moving across the row compares different patterns available to that same chain.

teaching.text: The **mode 1** column has the masses moving in the same direction. In **mode 2**, the left region moves against the right region. With an odd number of masses, the center can stay still while the two sides move against each other.
children: In **mode 3**, the middle region moves against the two outer regions. More highly divided patterns contain more changes in the direction of neighboring movement.

teaching.text: Higher modes involve more relative movement and stretching between connected parts, so their frequencies are higher. The spring properties stay the same; what changes is how strongly the pattern uses the springs.
children: In a chain with separate masses, the mode frequencies are generally **not exact whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency. Counting modes does not by itself establish a harmonic frequency pattern.

teaching.text: A **string** has mass and springiness throughout its length. Treating it as more and more small connected masses and springs approaches that continuous system.
children: In its first mode, the string moves as one main region. Higher modes divide it into more regions moving against each other.
Plucking a string can start several modes at once. Their motions add to produce the actual changing shape of the string, while controlled excitation can favor particular modes.

coverage.idea: N masses yield N modes and row/column meanings
Shared first/second/third mode patterns across chain sizes
More relative stretching gives higher frequencies
Separate-mass frequencies need not be harmonic multiples
Continuous string has mass and stiffness distributed along length
Real combined string motion and selective excitation

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** has no movement at either end. In its first mode, one main section rises and falls. In the second mode, two sections move against one another; in the third, three sections alternate.
The lowest mode has the **base frequency**. The higher frequencies are **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of that base.
children: Here the first mode is **100 Hz**, meaning 100 cycles per second. The second is **200 Hz** and completes two cycles while the first completes one. The third is 300 Hz and completes three.
The motion is slowed for viewing. The Hz values give the represented vibration rates, rather than the slow visible playback rate.

teaching.text: Several modes can vibrate **at the same time**. The combined string adds their displacements at every point, creating a changing shape that contains all of those frequencies.
A **spectrum** separates the combined vibration into its frequencies and amplitudes. **Frequency in Hz runs horizontally**, and **amplitude**, the strength of the measured movement, runs vertically.
children: The black dot marks the **pickup point**, the location where the string’s motion is measured. In this demonstration, the strengths were set so each of the five modes makes an equal-height peak there.
A peak’s horizontal position tells its rate; a taller peak means a stronger contribution, rather than a faster vibration.

teaching.text: Five active modes produce **five spectral spikes**. If only mode 3 is active, the spectrum has **one spike at 300 Hz**, with no contribution at the other four mode frequencies.
children: This lets a complex movement be understood in terms of which component vibrations are present and how strongly each contributes.

coverage.idea: Fixed endpoints and successive string patterns
Base frequency and consecutive whole-number harmonics
Hz and meaningful 100/200/300 comparison
Combined motion is sum of active modes
Spectrum axes, amplitude versus frequency, pickup and equal peaks
One active mode versus five active modes spectrum prediction

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a surface that can vibrate. Its connected moving parts extend in two directions, so a mode divides a surface into moving regions rather than dividing only a line.
The **two-number mode labels** describe how many regions occur in each direction.
children: In **(1, 1)**, the surface rises and falls as one region. In **(2, 1)**, two regions move against one another along one direction. In **(1, 2)**, the split is along the other direction.
In **(2, 2)**, four regions alternate. In **(3, 1)**, three regions alternate along one direction. Still lines separate regions moving in opposite directions.

teaching.text: The **All 5 modes** surface adds the five separate movements. The black **pickup point** identifies where its motion is measured, and the spectrum contains one spike for each active frequency.
children: The frequency axis is horizontal, and relative amplitude is vertical. The five equal heights mean equal measured contributions at that point.
The equally spaced frequencies were **assigned for this demonstration**. They are not calculated natural frequencies of the rectangular membrane.

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** are vibrating tissue with many connected moving parts. Several modes can contribute at once, and their combined vibration produces a voice signal containing several frequencies.

coverage.idea: Membrane extends in two directions
Actual two-index patterns (1,1),(2,1),(1,2),(2,2),(3,1)
Combined surface, pickup point and spectrum
Assigned frequencies are illustrative rather than natural rectangle frequencies
Vocal folds as connected vibrating tissue with simultaneous modes

teaching.text: **The scientific method** connects an account of how a system works with a measurement that can test it. A **theory** states the behavior clearly, often using **differential equations**, equations that describe how quantities change over time.
children: For a spring, the restoring relation predicts a pull toward equilibrium after stretching and a push toward equilibrium after compression. Solving the equations makes a specific behavioral prediction.

teaching.text: The voice model treats the **vocal folds as a membrane** with many connected masses and restoring forces. More parts require more interacting equations, but the same mass-and-stiffness reasoning explains why vibration occurs.
children: The prediction is that a **laryngeal vibration signal**, produced by vocal-fold vibration, will have a spectrum with **evenly spaced harmonics**.

teaching.text: Two voice recordings can test that prediction in **Praat**, a program for analyzing speech. A **spectral slice** shows which frequencies occur in a selected part of the recording.
children: One recorded voice has peaks near a low base frequency and its multiples. Another has a higher base frequency and peaks spaced farther apart.

Both support the same prediction when each voice’s peaks occur at regular intervals set by its own base frequency. The second harmonic is about twice the base, and the third about three times the base.

teaching.text: The position of a peak along the frequency axis gives its **frequency**. A higher base frequency is a faster rate of vibration, not necessarily a taller peak.
children: Differences in vocal-fold mass help explain differences in base frequency. With other properties unchanged, thinner folds with less mass can vibrate faster, producing a higher pitch and wider harmonic spacing.

teaching.text: The voice spectrum contributes to **recognizing a familiar voice**. Familiarity with a person includes familiarity with their vocal-fold vibration. Their vowel production contributes additional information through the resonances of the air in the vocal tract.

coverage.idea: Theory, differential equations and a measurable prediction
Vocal-fold membrane model predicts evenly spaced harmonics
Two recorded voices tested in Praat spectral slices
Individual base frequencies with the same harmonic relationship
Vocal-fold mass, pitch and harmonic spacing
Voice recognition and vocal-fold versus air contribution

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has one end that stays still and one end that can move. The fixed bottom is a **node**, a location with no movement throughout the cycle. The free top is an **antinode**, a location with the greatest movement.

The first mode goes from no movement at the bottom to maximum movement at the top. Higher modes add still points inside the system and more regions moving against one another, while preserving those endpoint conditions.
children: The allowed frequencies are **odd multiples of the base frequency**, one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. The endpoint conditions exclude the intervening even multiples.

In the example, mode 1 is 100 Hz and mode 2 is 300 Hz. **Mode 2 names the second allowed pattern**, while 300 Hz names its rate. The second allowed pattern is three times, rather than twice, the base frequency.

teaching.text: The fixed–free spectrum has four equal-height peaks when the four shown modes contribute equally. The positions at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz** show the odd-multiple frequency pattern; the heights show amplitude.

With **the same length and wave speed**, freeing one end halves the lowest frequency compared with fixing both ends. A fixed–fixed first mode occupies half a wave, while a fixed–free first mode occupies a quarter wave.
children: The examples can be tuned to share a chosen 100 Hz lowest frequency. That chosen setting does not remove the effect of changing an endpoint while holding length and wave speed fixed.

teaching.text: A **building** is fixed to the ground at its base while its upper part can sway. Its lowest mode has the structure moving together; higher modes involve more opposing movement between regions.
children: The physical distinction is how the structure moves relative to its fixed base. Favoring the lowest pattern avoids the stronger opposing movements between neighboring sections that occur in higher patterns.

coverage.idea: Fixed/free boundaries, node and antinode
Allowed odd multiples and higher internal patterns
Mode index versus harmonic multiple
Equal-height odd-frequency spectrum
Freeing one end halves lowest frequency at fixed length/wave speed
Illustrative retuning does not negate fixed-parameter comparison
Fixed-base free-top building behavior as direct application

teaching.text: **Stabilization** means bringing a changing system toward **equilibrium** and keeping its fluctuations from becoming too large. **Balancing feedback** counteracts a departure from that balance.
The economic example concerns **boom-bust cycles**, repeated swings in economic activity. The black curve represents **unemployment**, while the gray curve represents **inflation**.
children: The curves alternate, with one quantity rising while the other falls in the example. The fluctuation concerns both variables changing over time.
Their peaks and troughs show quantities changing over time. The hands pressing the curves down represent an attempt to make those fluctuations smaller.
**Damping** means reducing the size of an oscillation. Stabilization policy tries to reduce large swings that can produce high unemployment or rapidly rising prices.

teaching.text: **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, abbreviated **DSGE**, names a theory that includes change over time and unpredictable disturbances.
children: **Dynamic** refers to the system’s development over time. **Stochastic** refers to unpredictable shocks, events that disturb its course.
An unexpected disruption can push the system away from balance. A theory of stabilization asks how its interactions respond and whether the departure becomes smaller.

In **stochastic gradient descent, SGD**, data are selected randomly for learning. Random selection and unpredictable shocks are different sources of variation, but both uses of **stochastic** refer to randomness in the system.

teaching.text: **Microeconomic** activity consists of individual decisions, such as buying something or applying for work. **Macroeconomic** quantities describe the whole economy, including unemployment and inflation.
children: The connection concerns how many small interactions produce the larger behavior being measured. The important quantities are the changing economic variables, the disturbances and the response toward balance.

coverage.idea: Stabilization, equilibrium and balancing feedback
Boom-bust cycles and unemployment/inflation curve key
Damping reduces fluctuation magnitude
DSGE dynamic/stochastic terms and unpredictable shocks
Microeconomic decisions versus macroeconomic quantities
Stochastic also names randomness in SGD data selection without a worked analogy

teaching.text: A **mass-spring system** vibrates because its parts contribute different effects. The spring supplies a **restoring force** toward **equilibrium**, and the mass has **inertia**, so its movement continues.
children: Pulling the mass stretches the spring. After release, the spring pulls it back toward equilibrium. The mass still has motion when it reaches that position, so it passes through and compresses the spring.
The compressed spring pushes it back in the other direction. This interaction produces the repeating cycle.

teaching.text: The object’s **m** label names its mass. The central guide marks **equilibrium**, the reference position from which displacement is measured.
**Longitudinal motion** is along the spring line, left and right. **Transverse motion** is across that line, up and down between the supports.
children: In the transverse system, displacement stretches the supports and their restoring pull acts toward the middle. Continued motion takes the mass through that middle position.
Both systems have the same mass and total restoring stiffness, so they vibrate at the same rate. Their direction differs while their underlying mass-and-spring behavior stays the same.

coverage.idea: Restoring force and inertia produce vibration
Mass m and equilibrium reference position
Longitudinal/transverse motion and equal rates

teaching.text: **Frequency** counts complete back-and-forth cycles per second. The **Reference** row starts with mass **m** and total restoring stiffness **K**. Each other row changes one property while retaining the other.
The **Bigger mass** row has **4m**, four times the reference mass, with stiffness still K. The heavier mass is harder to turn around, so each complete cycle takes longer.
children: **Half the rate** means half as many cycles in the same time as the reference. It describes a lower frequency, rather than a smaller displacement.

teaching.text: The **Stiffer spring** row keeps mass m and uses **4K**, four times the reference stiffness. A stronger restoring pull turns the mass around sooner.
children: **Twice the rate** means twice as many cycles in the same time as the reference. It is a higher frequency.

teaching.text: These comparisons separate **more mass lowering frequency** from **more stiffness raising frequency**. The longitudinal and transverse versions match in each row, so the effects apply to either movement direction.

coverage.idea: Frequency and reference m/K settings
4m at unchanged K gives half rate with cause
4K at unchanged m gives twice rate with cause
Mass/stiffness effects in both directions

teaching.text: The two equal masses and three springs have **two modes of vibration**. A mode describes the pattern of the connected system. The numbers on the masses identify objects, while **mode 1 and mode 2** identify patterns.
In **mode 1**, the masses move together. Both go up and down together, or both go left and right together.
children: The middle spring keeps the same length because the masses’ separation does not change. Only the outer springs stretch and compress to provide the restoring action.

teaching.text: In **mode 2**, the masses move against each other. One rises as the other falls, or the two move toward and away from each other.
children: The middle spring now changes length as well. All three springs contribute, so this pattern uses more stiffness and has a **higher frequency**.
The masses and individual spring stiffnesses are unchanged between the two modes. The difference comes from how the pattern uses the springs.

teaching.text: Increasing the **middle spring’s stiffness** affects the modes differently. It leaves mode 1 unchanged because that spring does not stretch there. It raises mode 2’s frequency because the middle spring does stretch in that pattern.
Both modes can also occur together. Moving both masses away from equilibrium by different amounts combines the together pattern with the opposing pattern.
children: The **Both modes** row adds the two movements. Its changing shape contains two frequencies, rather than a new third mode.

coverage.idea: Whole-system modes versus mass identifiers
Mode 1 together and no middle-spring length change
Mode 2 opposed and extra restoring action raises frequency
Actual middle-spring stiffening comparison
Simultaneous modes and two-frequency combined movement

teaching.text: Three connected masses have **three modes**. In mode 1, they move together. In mode 2, the middle mass stays still while the outer masses move against each other. In mode 3, the middle mass moves against both outer masses.
children: The object numbers identify the three masses. The mode numbers identify different patterns of that same complete system.

teaching.text: The frequencies rise from mode 1 to mode 3 because the higher patterns involve stronger movement against neighboring parts and more stretching and compression.
children: In the lowest mode, the masses move mostly together and use less internal stiffness. In the highest mode, the center and outer masses move against one another and strongly change the connecting spring lengths.

teaching.text: A **local stiffness change** matters according to how much the changed spring stretches or compresses. Little stretching or compression means little effect; more stretching or compression means a larger increase in the mode’s frequency.
children: This distinguishes moving a spring along with its neighbors from changing its length. Stiffness contributes through the latter.

teaching.text: Making the **middle mass heavier** lowers the frequency of **mode 1**, because that mass moves in mode 1. The same mass increase leaves **mode 2 unchanged**, because the middle mass stays still in that pattern.
children: It also lowers **mode 3**. In this comparison the middle mass moves more strongly in mode 3 than in mode 1, so the frequency decrease is larger in mode 3.
The physical change stays at the same location. Different outcomes arise because each mode uses that location differently.

teaching.text: A mass’s influence on frequency therefore depends on **how much it moves in that mode**. No motion gives no mass effect, while stronger motion gives a stronger slowing effect.
children: The **All three** row combines the three patterns. Even in combined motion, each component mode retains its own pattern and frequency.

coverage.idea: Three actual movement patterns and object/mode identifiers
Frequency ordering from internal stretching
Local stiffness acts through deformation
Heavier middle mass lowers modes 1/3 but not 2
Greater mode-3 motion produces greater frequency drop
Combined three-mode movement

teaching.text: **N masses give N modes** in these chains. N is a count of the masses, not a measure of the mass of one object. The rows compare chains with different numbers of masses, while the columns compare their available patterns.

In **mode 1**, the masses move in the same direction. In **mode 2**, one region moves against the other; with an odd number of masses, the center stays still. In **mode 3**, the middle region moves against the two sides.
children: Moving across one row compares different patterns of the same system. Moving down a column follows the same kind of pattern across systems with different numbers of masses.

teaching.text: Higher modes use more relative movement between connected parts. Their springs stretch and compress more strongly, giving greater restoring action and higher frequencies.
children: The frequencies of a separate-mass chain are generally not exact whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency. The number of modes and the spacing of their frequencies are different properties.

teaching.text: A **string** has mass and springiness continuously along its length. Packing more and more small connected masses and springs into a model approaches that continuous system.
children: The first string mode moves as one main region, the second divides it into two opposing regions, and the third has the middle moving against the outer regions.

teaching.text: A string can move in **many modes at once**. Adding the separate patterns produces a complicated movement, even though each component mode has a simple form. A **pure tone** has only one frequency.
The **ear** also responds through structures with different vibration frequencies. This helps separate the frequency components arriving together from different instruments or voices.

coverage.idea: N-mode count and grid organization
First/second/third chain patterns
Relative stretching explains higher frequencies
Discrete-chain mode count versus harmonic spacing
Continuous string limit and spatial patterns
Combined modes and single-frequency pure tone
Auditory mass-spring response to simultaneous frequencies

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** cannot move at either end. Its lowest-frequency pattern has one main moving section between those still ends. That section is a **half-wave packet**.
The lowest mode’s rate is the **base frequency**. Higher patterns fit two, three or more half-wave packets into the **same string length**.
children: In mode 2, two neighboring sections move against each other. Fitting two packets into the same length gives twice the base frequency.
Mode 3 fits three packets and has three times the base frequency. The resulting whole-number multiples are **harmonics**.

teaching.text: The represented frequencies are **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**. **Hertz** means cycles per second, so the 200 Hz mode repeats twice as often as the 100 Hz mode.
children: These frequencies identify the rates of the patterns. The animation is slowed so that the movement can be followed.

teaching.text: The combined string adds the displacements of the active modes at each point. Its motion can be complicated because several frequencies occur together.
A **spectrum** shows frequency along the horizontal axis and **amplitude**, the strength of the measured vibration, along the vertical axis.
children: The black **pickup point** is the location where motion is measured. The five peaks have equal heights because each mode was set to contribute equally at that point.
Peak height measures contribution, while horizontal position measures rate. Equal-height peaks can have different frequencies.

coverage.idea: Fixed endpoints and first half-wave pattern
Base frequency and half-wave fit yields harmonic multiples
Hz values and slow display versus physical frequency
Exact combined modal motion
Spectrum axes and pickup equal-amplitude peaks

teaching.text: **Increasing mass lowers frequency, while increasing stiffness raises it.** Mass is written **m**, and stiffness is written **k** or **K**. The arrows indicate increases and decreases.
children: More mass is harder to turn around. More stiffness gives a stronger restoring pull for the same displacement. The first printed line has a downward arrow beside stiffness by mistake; the stiffness principle below gives the correct upward effect.

teaching.text: An **n-mass system has n modes**. Here n counts masses and available whole-system patterns. Three connected masses therefore have three modes, with each mode specifying how all three move.
children: Higher modes involve stronger relative movement and more stretching between neighbors, so their frequencies are higher. A mode number identifies a pattern, rather than an individual mass.

teaching.text: **Increasing a particular mass lowers a mode’s frequency according to how much that mass moves in the mode.** A mass that stays still has no slowing effect when made heavier.
children: At the fixed ends of a string there is no motion, so added mass there leaves the mode unchanged. At a strongly moving location, added mass has a larger effect on lowering frequency.

teaching.text: **The regions of greatest movement and greatest stretching are different regions.** A region can travel a long way while keeping nearly the same spacing between neighboring parts.
children: Around a still point, neighboring parts can stretch and compress strongly. A point staying still therefore does not mean there is no spring action around it.

teaching.text: **Increasing a spring’s stiffness raises a mode’s frequency according to how much the spring stretches and compresses.** The location matters because each mode has its own pattern of stretching and compression.
children: Where a spring does not change length, stiffening it has no effect in that ideal pattern. Strong stretching or compression allows increased stiffness to raise frequency more strongly.

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** stays still at both ends. Its **base frequency** is the frequency of its lowest mode, which contains one **half-wave packet**, a moving section between two still points.
children: Higher modes fit two, three or more such sections into the same string length. The second fits two and vibrates twice as fast; the third fits three and vibrates three times as fast.
These whole-number multiples are **harmonics**. The packet count explains the frequency pattern, rather than requiring a separate rule for every mode.

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** stays still at one end and moves freely at the other. The still end is a **node**, and the freely moving end is an **antinode**, where motion is greatest. Its first mode contains one **quarter-wave packet** from node to antinode.
children: Higher allowed modes contain **one, three, five or seven quarter-wave packets** in the same length. An even count would finish at a still point rather than the moving free end, so only odd counts satisfy the endpoint conditions.

The frequencies are **odd multiples of the base frequency**. Mode 2 is the second allowed pattern, with three quarter-wave packets and three times the base frequency. The mode number and the frequency multiple therefore describe different things.

coverage.idea: Principle 1 mass lowers/stiffness raises frequency with symbols and printed typo
Principle 2 n masses n modes and frequency ordering
Principle 3 local mass effect depends on modal motion
Principle 4 maximal movement versus maximal deformation locations
Principle 5 local stiffness effect depends on stretching/compression
Principle 6 fixed-fixed base frequency and half-wave fit yields whole harmonics
Principle 7 fixed-free node/antinode quarter-wave fit yields odd multiples
Mode index differs from harmonic frequency multiple

teaching.text: A vibrating string has **different locations for strongest movement and strongest stretching**. In the first mode, movement is greatest near the middle and vanishes at the fixed ends.
children: Near the middle, neighboring parts mostly travel together. They can move far without much change in their separation.
Near a fixed end, the neighboring moving material pulls against a location that stays still. This creates strong stretching and compression even though the fixed point does not move.

teaching.text: Higher modes repeat the alternation along the string. Regions with strong motion are separated by regions with strong stretching and little displacement.
children: A **node** stays still throughout the cycle. That is different from a moving point passing through equilibrium for one instant.

teaching.text: The effect of a local change must be matched to **the particular mode**. A location that moves in one mode can remain still in another, so adding mass there can lower one frequency and leave another unchanged.
children: Added stiffness instead matters where neighboring parts change their spacing. The source of the frequency change is the part’s role in the pattern, rather than its location alone.

teaching.text: The combined string and spectrum show two ways of describing the vibration. The string shows movement at locations; the spectrum separates its **frequency components** and **amplitudes**.
children: The black point marks where the spectrum’s movement was measured. The Hz values give component rates, while peak heights give their contributions at that point.

Alternating motion/deformation in higher modes

teaching.text: The **green box marks one location** on the string, shown in two different modes. **Mode 4** moves strongly at that location, while **mode 5** has a still point there with strong stretching around it.
children: The 400 Hz and 500 Hz labels give the example’s starting frequencies. Both mass and stiffness are increased at the same marked section, with the rest of the string unchanged.

teaching.text: In **mode 4**, added **mass** lowers frequency because the marked section moves. A heavier moving part is harder to turn around.
children: Increasing **stiffness** there contributes little because the section does little stretching or compressing. The overall result for mode 4 is a **frequency decrease**.

teaching.text: In **mode 5**, added mass has no effect because the marked point stays still. The mass increase cannot slow motion that is absent from that point in this mode.
children: Increasing stiffness raises the frequency because neighboring parts stretch and compress strongly around that still point. The overall result for mode 5 is a **frequency increase**.

teaching.text: The combined change therefore gives **mode 4 down and mode 5 up**. The same added mass and stiffness have different effects because the two modes use the location differently.
children: **m** means mass and **k** means stiffness in the written answer. The two tendencies do not cancel automatically; their influence depends on the movement and changes in spacing between neighboring parts at that location.

teaching.text: Predicting a small local change in this way is **perturbation**. A drum demonstration adds wax to selected locations, increasing their mass.
children: Wax placed at a strongly moving region lowers the frequency. Wax placed at a still point leaves that mode’s frequency unchanged. The change can be detected by the resulting sound even when the movement is too fast to see.

teaching.text: The vibrating **vocal folds** have many connected moving parts. A **membrane** model extends those parts across a surface, allowing vibration patterns in two directions.
The mode pair **(1, 1)** describes one moving region in each direction. **(2, 1)** and **(1, 2)** divide the surface into opposing regions along different directions.
children: **(2, 2)** gives four alternating regions, and **(3, 1)** gives three regions along one direction. Still lines separate regions that move against one another.
The pair identifies the spatial pattern. Its separate **Hz** value identifies the vibration frequency.

teaching.text: The **All 5 modes** surface adds the five component patterns. A black **pickup point** identifies where the combined movement is measured.
children: The spectrum places **frequency horizontally** and **relative amplitude vertically**. Its five equal-height spikes show equal measured contributions at that pickup point.

The displayed harmonic frequencies are **assigned teaching values**, not the natural frequencies calculated for the rectangular membrane. The combined movement still equals the sum of the separate motions.

teaching.text: A **theory** describes how a system works, often through **differential equations** that express change over time. A **prediction** states what a measurement should show if that description is right.
The vocal-fold model has many connected masses and restoring forces. Their combined vibration is predicted to produce **harmonics**, evenly spaced spectral peaks at multiples of a base frequency.
children: The **base frequency** belongs to the lowest component. Higher harmonics occur at twice, three times and further whole-number multiples of that frequency.

teaching.text: A **spectral slice in Praat** tests the prediction on a recorded voice. The measured second peak is about twice the frequency of the first, and the third is about three times the first.
children: Each person can have a different base frequency. The prediction concerns the relationship between peaks within the same voice, rather than one frequency shared by every voice.

teaching.text: Local changes to the vocal folds’ **mass and stiffness** can alter the vibration. A **nodule** adds tissue mass at a particular location, and smoking can change the properties of different parts of the folds.
children: Different modes move different amounts at that location, so the same local change can shift them by different amounts. The resulting change in the spectrum contributes to a change in the sound of the voice.

coverage.idea: Theory/differential-equation/prediction connection
Vocal-fold harmonics and individual base frequencies
Praat spectral slice confirms approximate multiples
Nodules and local vocal-fold mass/stiffness changes affect modes

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has a **node** at its fixed end and an **antinode** at its free end. A node stays still throughout vibration, while an antinode has the greatest movement.
The first mode contains one **quarter-wave packet**, running from no movement at the fixed end to maximum movement at the free end.
children: The next allowed mode fits three such packets into the same length, and the following mode fits five. Adding two packets preserves a moving free end; an even packet count would place a still point there.
The frequencies therefore follow **one, three, five and seven times the base frequency**. The second allowed mode has three times the lowest frequency, rather than twice it.

teaching.text: The example spectrum has peaks at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**. Those positions give the frequencies; their equal heights give the equal contributions selected for this demonstration.
children: For the same length and wave speed, freeing one end **halves the lowest frequency** compared with fixing both ends. A chosen tuning can make two examples share a lowest value without reversing that fixed-parameter comparison.

teaching.text: In the idealized **vocal tract**, air is fixed at the **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds, and free at the lips.
children: The closed vocal-fold end prevents the adjacent air from moving back and forth. The open lip end permits that motion. These are conditions on the air’s movement, not instructions that the whole tract must remain motionless.
The air can vibrate in several modes at once. Changing the tongue and lips changes local air properties and shifts the resonances used in different speech sounds.

teaching.text: A **building** has a fixed base and a top that can sway. Its first mode moves the structure together, while higher modes contain more opposing movement between regions.
children: Designing the structure to favor the lowest pattern limits the stronger opposing movements between neighboring sections that occur in higher patterns. Fixed and free refer to the movement possible at the two ends.

Odd-packet fit yields odd frequency multiples and mode-number distinction

teaching.text: The air in the **vocal tract** has both **mass** and **springiness**. The masses in the chain represent the air’s **inertia**, its resistance to changes in motion. The springs represent the restoring action that appears when air is compressed.
children: The uniform tube uses identical masses and coupling properties along its length. The fixed glottal end is on the left, and the free lip end is on the right.

teaching.text: The upper row is **mode 1**, associated with the **first formant, F1**. Its movement is smallest at the fixed end and grows toward the free end.
children: The lower row is **mode 2**, associated with the **second formant, F2**. Its movement includes an additional still location inside the tube.
The two rows represent the same air column in two different patterns. They are not two different vocal tracts.

teaching.text: A **formant** is a resonance of the air in the tract, a frequency at which that air responds strongly. **F1 and F2 order the resonances** from lowest to next lowest.
children: In the uniform fixed–free tube, F2 is **three times F1**, because the next allowed pattern fits three quarter-wave sections rather than one. The 2 in F2 identifies the second resonance, not twice the first frequency.

teaching.text: The position marks locate modeled constrictions. **1/3 /a/** is one third of the distance from the glottis toward the lips, **2/3 /i/** is two thirds, and **/u/** marks the lip end.
children: These fractions measure location along the tract. A location can take part differently in the two modes, so changing air properties there can affect F1 and F2 differently.

coverage.idea: Air inertia and springiness represented by chain
Uniform tube and glottal/lip endpoint orientation

Formant definition and resonance ordering

1/3 and 2/3 distances with vowel constriction locations

teaching.text: A **constriction** is a narrowing in the **vocal tract**. The tongue and lips change where the passage narrows, and that location helps distinguish vowels.
**High** and **low** describe tongue height. **Front**, **central** and **back** describe how far forward or backward the tongue is.
children: These terms locate tongue position. They do not refer to high or low voice pitch.

teaching.text: The high front vowel in **Dean** has a constriction near **two thirds of the distance from the glottis**. The glottis is the opening between the vocal folds, so the distance is measured from the lower end of the tract toward the lips.
children: The low back vowel in **Don** has a constriction near **one third** of that distance, farther toward the back of the tract.

teaching.text: In **Dune**, the tongue is high and back and the lips are rounded, creating a constriction at the lip end. **Done** is the central example with no marked narrowing, while **Dan** is low and front with no constriction position marked.

The same constriction location can have strong air motion in one mode and strong compression in another. Vowel effects therefore depend on **where the narrowing acts in each mode**, rather than on narrowing alone.

teaching.text: The two chains represent the **same air column in two modes**. The upper row is **mode 1/F1**, and the lower row is **mode 2/F2**. Both have the same fixed glottal end and open lip end.

The circles represent mass in the air, while the connecting springs make its springiness visible. **Motion** is the back-and-forth travel of a part. **Compression** is the decrease in spacing between neighboring parts, and expansion is an increase in that spacing.
children: Nearby parts can move together without changing their separation very much. This gives strong motion with little compression.
Around a still point, neighboring parts can move toward and away from one another. There can therefore be strong compression even where local movement is small.

teaching.text: The patterns place their motion and compression differently. **Near the lips, both modes move strongly**. Farther inside the tract, one mode can move strongly where the other compresses strongly.
children: A change in local mass matters when that location moves. A change in local stiffness matters when neighboring parts compress or stretch. One local change can consequently affect the two resonances differently.

teaching.text: The **1/3 /a/** and **2/3 /i/** marks give positions measured from the glottis toward the lips. The **/u/** mark locates the free lip end.
children: The fractions describe distances; F1 and F2 name resonances. Comparing the same marked position in both rows shows how the role of a location depends on the mode.

coverage.idea: Same fixed-free air column compared in mode1/F1 and mode2/F2
Motion versus compression/expansion between neighboring parts

teaching.text: For **/u/**, lip rounding narrows the air passage at the **free lip end**. In the model, the masses near that end become heavier. This is called **loading the free end**.
children: The larger blue masses identify the changed region. The upper and lower rows apply that same change to mode 1 and mode 2.

teaching.text: Both modes have **strong back-and-forth motion near the lips**. Neighboring parts move mostly together there, so their compression is small.
Increasing the mass at a strongly moving location makes the cycle slower. **F1 and F2 both decrease**, because that location moves strongly in both patterns.
children: Narrowing also increases effective stiffness, but little compression occurs at the lip end, so its stiffness effect is weak compared with the mass effect.

teaching.text: The arrows **F1 ↓ and F2 ↓** describe lower resonance frequencies. They do not describe the direction in which the air travels; the air still vibrates back and forth along the tract.

coverage.idea: /u/ lip narrowing and free-end loading
Same changed masses in both modal rows
Strong lip-end motion with little compression in both modes
Local added mass lowers both F1/F2 and stiffness contributes little
Down arrows identify resonance-frequency changes

teaching.text: The modeled **/i/** constriction is near **two thirds of the distance from the glottis toward the lips**. The highlighted region identifies the same changed location in both rows.
children: A constriction raises both the effective mass and stiffness of the air there. The two tendencies do not automatically cancel because their influence depends on the mode.

teaching.text: In **mode 1**, the location has strong motion and relatively little compression. Added moving mass slows the vibration, so **F1 decreases**.
In **mode 2**, the same location has strong compression and expansion. Increasing stiffness strengthens the restoring action, so **F2 increases**.
The result is **F1 ↓ and F2 ↑**. The arrows indicate opposite changes in resonance frequency, produced by one narrowing of the tract.
children: The first and second formants are affected differently because a particular location has different movement and compression in their two modes.

coverage.idea: /i/ 2/3 location measured from glottis
One constriction changes both local mass and stiffness

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the modeled constriction is near **one third of the distance from the glottis**. The highlighted region marks the same local increase in effective mass and stiffness in both rows.
In **mode 1**, compression and expansion are strong at that location. The stiffness increase provides a stronger restoring action, so **F1 increases**.
In **mode 2**, back-and-forth motion is strong there. The mass increase slows that vibration, so **F2 decreases**.
The combined result is **F1 ↑ and F2 ↓**. This is a different outcome from a constriction near two thirds of the tract length because the mode patterns use those locations differently.
children: The rule stays the same: added moving mass lowers a resonance, while added stiffness where air compresses raises it. The location determines which contribution is stronger for each mode.

coverage.idea: /a/ 1/3 constriction position measured from glottis
Mode1 stiffness effect raises F1
Mode2 mass effect lowers F2
Same conceptual rule gives opposite vowel-specific outcome

teaching.text: **Increasing mass lowers frequency, while increasing stiffness raises it.** Mass is written **m**, and stiffness is written **k** or **K**. The arrows indicate increases and decreases.
children: More mass is harder to turn around. More stiffness gives a stronger restoring pull for the same displacement. The first printed line has a downward arrow beside stiffness by mistake; the stiffness principle below gives the correct upward effect.

teaching.text: An **n-mass system has n modes**. Here n counts masses and available whole-system patterns. Three connected masses therefore have three modes, with each mode specifying how all three move.
children: Higher modes involve stronger relative movement and more stretching between neighbors, so their frequencies are higher. A mode number identifies a pattern, rather than an individual mass.

teaching.text: **Increasing a particular mass lowers a mode’s frequency according to how much that mass moves in the mode.** A mass that stays still has no slowing effect when made heavier.
children: At the fixed ends of a string there is no motion, so added mass there leaves the mode unchanged. At a strongly moving location, added mass has a larger effect on lowering frequency.

teaching.text: **The regions of greatest movement and greatest stretching are different regions.** A region can travel a long way while keeping nearly the same spacing between neighboring parts.
children: Around a still point, neighboring parts can stretch and compress strongly. A point staying still therefore does not mean there is no spring action around it.

teaching.text: **Increasing a spring’s stiffness raises a mode’s frequency according to how much the spring stretches and compresses.** The location matters because each mode has its own pattern of stretching and compression.
children: Where a spring does not change length, stiffening it has no effect in that ideal pattern. Strong stretching or compression allows increased stiffness to raise frequency more strongly.

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** stays still at both ends. Its **base frequency** is the frequency of its lowest mode, which contains one **half-wave packet**, a moving section between two still points.
children: Higher modes fit two, three or more such sections into the same string length. The second fits two and vibrates twice as fast; the third fits three and vibrates three times as fast.
These whole-number multiples are **harmonics**. The packet count explains the frequency pattern, rather than requiring a separate rule for every mode.

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** stays still at one end and moves freely at the other. The still end is a **node**, and the freely moving end is an **antinode**, where motion is greatest. Its first mode contains one **quarter-wave packet** from node to antinode.
children: Higher allowed modes contain **one, three, five or seven quarter-wave packets** in the same length. An even count would finish at a still point rather than the moving free end, so only odd counts satisfy the endpoint conditions.

The frequencies are **odd multiples of the base frequency**. Mode 2 is the second allowed pattern, with three quarter-wave packets and three times the base frequency. The mode number and the frequency multiple therefore describe different things.

The uniform vocal-tract model has a fixed glottal end and free lip end. Its air resonances are **formants**. A constriction changes those resonances by changing the local mass and stiffness in the different modes.

teaching.text: The air moves **lengthwise**, back and forth along the tube. The small blue circles represent groups of air molecules, with the closed glottal end on the left and the open lips on the right.
**Motion** and **compression** describe different features. Motion is how far a part travels, while compression is how much closer neighboring parts become.
children: Lines that travel together can move strongly while keeping nearly the same separation. Where neighboring lines crowd together and spread apart, there is strong compression and expansion.
At a motion node, a line stays still, but neighboring air can move toward and away from it. Strong compression can therefore occur around a still point.

teaching.text: The **Schwa** row shows the uniform-tube example. The rows labeled **Mode 1 @ F1**, **Mode 2 @ F2** and **Mode 3 @ F3** separate the component air-motion patterns.
children: F1, F2 and F3 order the air resonances from lowest to highest. Their numbers name those resonances rather than individual air particles.

teaching.text: In the first mode, the closed end has little motion and strong compression, while the open lip end has strong motion and little compression. Higher modes fit more alternating regions into the same tract length.
A constriction can fall in a moving region for one mode and a compressing region for another. It can therefore lower one formant through added mass and raise another through added stiffness.
children: The effect follows the motion and compression at the changed location in each mode, rather than a rule that narrowing must move all formants in the same direction.

mappingFixes: L12p9 and p22 each explain all seven displayed principles. PDF Section9 final two bullets, on combined PDF page11, are not withheld from p9 or isolated on p22.
L11p4 integrates the full two-mass middle-spring/higher-frequency explanation from PDF pages2–3. L11p5 explains the actual spoken three-mass quiz rather than leaving the source prompt unexplained.
L12p18 includes both modal air movement/compression and the vowel-position labels, rather than only a paragraph listing positions.
Shared demonstrations are explained on each source occurrence. Source images, media, existing editions, interface and saved identities remain untouched.
sourceResolution: The native three-mass animation has unequal modal amplitudes. Mode1 is described as relatively little internal stretching rather than falsely asserting that both inner springs never change length.

The two-mass middle-spring stiffening discussion is placed on L12p5, where the exact unchanged-first-mode claim applies. L12p6 explains its general deformation principle and the actual three-mass center-loading comparison.

The membrane patterns follow the primary mode-pair labels (1,1),(2,1),(1,2),(2,2),(3,1), rather than the PDF’s less precise description of its third numbered panel. Assigned harmonic frequencies remain identified as illustrative.
The L12 printed stiffness-down arrow is explained as a source typo without modifying the original slide.

L12 vocal-tract/vowel pages are grounded in their primary slides/media and the PDF. No later verbal lines are attributed to the October13 transcript when that recording has not reached those explanations.
Spoken evidence uses explicit verified line ranges, with source-page/PDF coverage separately identified. The review does not claim that all PDF expansions were spoken on the matching date.

The economic example retains the taught dynamic/stochastic, micro/macro and balancing-feedback meanings, but removes the cross-domain x/v and numerical SGD-shock analogies rather than adding them as required learning.

review.writingReview: Retains the PDF’s substantive movement, spring-action, spectrum, testing and application explanations while rewriting personification, coaching, classroom narration and cross-slide roadmaps.
